newsitem.title: CHINA: Ex-Merrill man in court over HK money laundering charge.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Merrill man in court over HK money laundering charge.

text.p: Hong Kong police slapped money laundering charges on former Merrill Lynch private banking star Kevin Wallace on Wednesday, but he was freed on bail after an official from National Australia Bank handed over his surety.
Wallace, a 46-year-old American, appeared in court after police charged him with "dealing with the proceeds of an indictable offence", legal jargon for money laundering.
The offence falls under article 25 of Hong Kong's Organised and Serious Crimes Ordinance, with a maximum penalty of a HK$5 million ($646,000) fine and up to 14 years in prison. No plea was entered.

The charges relate to the transfer of more than HK$7 million from an account at Merrill Lynch International Bank in Singapore to National Australia Bank in Sydney to Hongkong Bank in this territory, senior government counsel Lynda Shine told reporters outside the court.
Dressed in a dark suit with a blue shirt and no tie, Wallace stood in the dock as Shine told the court the case was "serious and complicated". Proceedings were adjourned until October 16.
Hong Kong's Justice Department will now build its case, which would include interviews in Singapore and Australia and the tracing of funds, Shine said.
As conditions of bail, magistrate James Lee ordered Wallace to produce HK$500,000 in cash plus a third-party surety of HK$500,000, to surrender his passport and report to police once a week.
Wallace was also told not to interfere with witnesses anywhere in the world, nor to leave Hong Kong.

The HK$500,000 third-party surety was provided by Christopher Malone, who told the court he was the Hong Kong-based head of trade finance for the Asia region at National Australia Bank, one of Australia's most respected financial institutions.
Malone told Reuters he had known Wallace for five years and was acting as a friend in posting the surety from his own money.
"I was acting as a private individual. This is no connection with National Australia Bank," Malone said.
Merrill Lynch started civil proceedings against Wallace last month in Singapore and Hong Kong, and the company has filed a criminal complaint in Singapore.
The U.S. investment bank accused Wallace of engaging in unauthorised trading, misrepresenting or falsifying private clients' statements and forging client signatures.
Shine said the "charge in Hong Kong arises out of the offence in Singapore".
Wallace was seized by Hong Kong's Commercial Crime Bureau 10 days ago along with an unidentified Chinese and posted bail of more than HK$1 million on July 9.
The charge was laid after Wallace reported to police on Wednesday morning, a condition of his bail.
Wallace was employed by Merrill Lynch from late 1991 until his dismissal on May 15 this year.
In his job, Wallace acted as a financial consultant to wealthy clients across Asia, taking investment orders and providing investment advice.
Industry sources have said his clients were believed to have bank balances ranging from a few million to US$25 million.
Merrill Lynch has not commented on the sum involved, but industry sources have put it at around US$30 million.
The investment bank has said the costs it might incur from the alleged fraud would not be "significant to Merrill Lynch's business or financial position".
The company made a US$1.6 billion profit last year.
Merrill spokesman Robert Grieves said earlier the investment bank had settled with about half of Wallace's clients.
